implementation_notes: Scala's stream libraries carry the pattern: with Akka Streams (or its Apache Pekko fork) a Source.queue materialises the event inlet, Flow.scan folds events into the current state, and BroadcastHub fans the state out to many consumer Sources, while the API's point is bounded buffering and back-pressure so state production cannot outrun the consumers. Subscribers that must render immediately take the running value or a replayed snapshot; alternatively a typed actor can own the state and publish snapshots with only the fan-out in the stream. Choose the stream form when the state must be joined with other asynchronous sources - here the stream library is the framework, not a hand-rolled observer list.
code_sketch:
val (queue, source) =
  Source.queue[Event](bufferSize = 32, OverflowStrategy.dropNew).preMaterialize()

val stateSource: Source[State, NotUsed] =
  source.scan(State.Idle)(reduce)                  // pure (state, event)
        .toMat(BroadcastHub.sink[State](256))(Keep.right)
        .run()

// dispatch: queue.offer(Submit)   (dropped events surface in the failed Future)
// view:     stateSource.runWith(Sink.foreach(render))
pitfalls: Overflow strategies are lossy by design: Source.queue with dropNew, dropHead or dropBuffer drops events, and only dropNew reports the drop through the offer Future - choose per event type and log drops.
Every materialised stream needs a Materializer and must be run and later killed; an abandoned stream graph keeps its buffers and stages allocated.
BroadcastHub applies back-pressure by dropping for the slowest subscriber once its buffer fills, so a slow consumer can silently miss states - size it for the slowest consumer or conflate.
scan offers no replay: a consumer attaching later starts from the seed unless the current state is re-injected, so keep the latest value outside the stream as well.
